chief_complaint: painful blisters on palm after grease spill
hpi_details: A 32-year-old woman presents soon after a grease spill with painful blisters on her palm. The burn needs in-person assessment of depth, extent, sensation, circulation, and hand function.
ideas: thinks this is a hand burn
concerns: She is worried that the blisters will heal into tight scars that make her hand stiff and prevent her from typing at work next week.
expectations: She hopes to receive strong pain medication, soothing burn cream, and a sterile dressing so she can continue using her hand.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Thermal Burn Injury evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Thermal Burn Injury is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Management is guided by burn depth, extent, neurovascular status, tetanus status, and hand function; hand burns merit burn-specialist input.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: painful blisters on palm after grease spill

Key HPI features: A 32-year-old woman presents soon after a grease spill with painful blisters on her palm. The burn needs in-person assessment of depth, extent, sensation, circulation, and hand function.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Partial-Thickness Burn hand.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Thermal Burn Injury.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Chemical burn without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Inhalation injury (soot in mouth, hoarseness).
management_principles: Cool the burn with running water if still within a useful early window; do not apply ice. Assess depth, extent, circulation, sensation, and tetanus status.
Use clinician-selected analgesia and nonadherent dressings; blister management depends on location, depth, contamination, and local protocol.
Obtain burn-specialist input for a hand burn and urgently escalate numbness, pale or cool digits, severe swelling, infection, or breathing symptoms.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presents soon after a grease spill with painful blisters on the palm.
reference_soap.objective: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Partial-Thickness Burn hand.
reference_soap.assessment: Thermal hand burn; depth and neurovascular status require in-person assessment before confirming partial-thickness injury.
reference_soap.plan: Cool with running water if appropriate; do not apply ice. Assess burn depth, extent, circulation, sensation, tetanus status, and hand function. Use clinician-selected analgesia and dressings and obtain burn-specialist input because the hand is involved. Urgently reassess numbness, pale or cool digits, severe swelling, infection, or breathing symptoms.

teaching.one_liner: Tissue injury caused by heat exposure, requiring assessment of total body surface area (TBSA), depth, and airway involvement.

must_ask.say: What caused the burn — open flame, hot liquid, steam, or chemicals?
Were you trapped in an enclosed space, and do you have hoarseness or black soot in your cough?
Which body parts were burned — face, chest, arms, or legs?
Are the burned areas extremely painful and blistered, or numb and white?
Did you cool the burn with clean tap water and have you received IV fluids?

history.answer: Hot cooking grease splashed directly onto my right palm while I was cooking dinner about an hour ago, and now I have painful blisters.
I was pan-frying food when the hot cooking oil popped and splattered straight into my open right palm.
It happened about an hour ago, right around six o'clock this evening.
It is only on the center of my right palm, covering an area about the size of a small lemon.
I immediately put my hand under cool running tap water for about ten to fifteen minutes. I didn't apply any ice, butter, or ointment.
It is a very sharp, intense burning pain, around an eight out of ten. Touching it or exposing it to room air makes it sting terribly.
No, there are no numb or painless patches at all; the entire blistered skin hurts intensely.
No, the oil was fresh vegetable oil from a clean frying pan, and no dirt or debris got into it.
No, there is no bleeding at all. The blisters swelled up quickly with clear fluid and are still intact.
I can bend and straighten all my fingers, though stretching my palm pulls on the burn and hurts. My fingertips do not feel numb or tingly.
No, there was no open flame or smoke. I don't have any hoarseness, cough, difficulty breathing, or black phlegm.
No, I was standing in my open kitchen and there was no building fire or confined smoke.
No, it just happened an hour ago, so there is no foul odor, yellow pus, spreading redness, or fever.
I haven't had any IV fluids, but I drank a large glass of water right after it happened and I do not feel dizzy.
No, it was purely an accidental splash while cooking dinner.
I had a tetanus booster shot about four years ago when I scraped my knee.
I do not have any chronic medical illnesses like diabetes, poor circulation, or high blood pressure.
I have never had any surgeries and have never been hospitalized.
I don't take any prescription medicines, steroids, over-the-counter painkillers, or blood thinners.
I have no known allergies to medications, latex, or adhesive bandages.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used tobacco products.
I only drink a glass or two of wine socially on weekends.
I work as an accountant in an office, and I live in an apartment with my husband.
Both of my parents are healthy with no major medical conditions.
My last menstrual period started two weeks ago and was normal. We use condoms, and there is no chance that I am pregnant.
I realize this is a second-degree burn from the hot cooking oil, which is why blisters formed so fast.
I'm worried my hand will heal tight and stiff, so I won't be able to type or use a computer for my job next week.
I'm hoping to get some strong pain relief, soothing burn ointment, and a protective bandage so I can still use my hand.

exam.finding: The patient is alert, oriented, and visibly uncomfortable, gently cradling her right hand.
Blood pressure 118/76 mmHg, heart rate 82 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, body temperature 36.8°C, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Nasal passages and oral pharynx are pink and clear with no soot deposits, mucosal edema, or singed facial hair.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally on auscultation without wheezing, stridor, or crackles.
A 5 by 4 cm erythematous area on the right palm with multiple intact, fluid-filled blisters that are exquisitely tender, with no pale leathery areas or circumferential involvement.
Radial and ulnar pulses are 2+ and equal bilaterally, with capillary refill under 2 seconds in all digits.
Light touch sensation and two-point discrimination are intact and symmetric across all digits of the right hand.
Active finger flexion and extension are intact with full strength, though extending the palm elicits mild local discomfort.
All wrist and interphalangeal joints demonstrate full range of motion without intrinsic swelling or joint-line tenderness.
